teach.title: Passive clothes, active work

notice.ask: Which verb in each sentence looks passive but tells you what the ship, and Lydia, actually do?

teach.say: Some verbs have nothing but passive-shaped endings and yet mean something the subject does: **a deponent verb (passive-looking endings, active meaning: loquitur = he speaks)**. *sequitur* is not 'he is followed' but 'he follows'; *verētur* is 'he fears'. *Puerī magistrum sequuntur* — the boys follow the teacher.

check.ask: Which word here has a passive-looking ending and yet tells you what the sailor does?

teach.title: The singular endings: -or, -ris, -tur
teach.say: The endings are the passive set. *sequor* I follow, *sequeris* you follow, *sequitur* he or she follows. Every one has an *r* in it, and that *r* is the whole signal — but read the meaning as active anyway.

check.ask: Fill the three singular cells for sequor: I follow, you follow, he follows.

teach.title: The plural: -mur, -minī, -ntur
teach.say: *sequimur* we follow, *sequiminī* you all follow, *sequuntur* they follow. *-minī* is the odd one out with no *r* at all, so learn it by itself; *-ntur* is just the *-nt* of 'they' with *-ur* added.

check.ask: Fill the three plural cells for sequor: we follow, you all follow, they follow.

teach.title: The infinitive ends in -ī, never -re
teach.say: The infinitive (the plain 'to' form) of a deponent is the passive-shaped one: *sequī* to follow, *loquī* to speak, *cōnārī* to try, *verērī* to fear. An ordinary verb would say *sequere*. This is the quickest test there is: if the dictionary gives *-ī* or *-rī* where you expect *-re*, the verb is deponent.

check.ask: Nauta nāvem magnam ____ cōnātur. Write the infinitive of sequor.

teach.title: A deponent can take an object
teach.say: A real passive has no object — nobody is 'praised the teacher'. A deponent can have one, because its meaning is active: *discipulus magistrum verētur*, the pupil fears the teacher, with *magistrum* in the accusative (the object form). An accusative sitting beside a *-tur* verb is nearly always the sign of a deponent.

check.ask: sequuntur: what person, number and voice is it, and which word in the sentence is its object?

teach.title: Telling it from a real passive
teach.say: *vocātur* and *loquitur* end alike, but *vocātur* is the passive (the 'is done' form), he is called, while *loquitur* means he speaks. Two things settle it: a doer named with *ā* or *ab* belongs to a passive, and the dictionary says whether an active exists at all — *vocō* does, *loquō* does not.

check.ask: vocantur and sequuntur end the same way. Which one is the boys' own doing?

core.text: Some verbs wear passive clothes but do active work: **a deponent verb (passive-looking endings, active meaning: loquitur = he speaks)**. *Lydia eum sequitur* — Lydia follows him; *nauta Neptūnum verētur* — the sailor fears Neptune. Their endings are the passive ones (*-or, -ris, -tur, -mur, -minī, -ntur*), their infinitive ends in *-rī* or *-ī* (*loquī* to speak, *sequī* to follow, *verērī* to fear), and there is no active form at all. The dictionary lists them by the first person: *loquor, sequor, proficīscor* (set out). Latin name: verba dēpōnentia.
Think of English *he is gone*: passive shape, but it only means he went. A deponent has 'laid aside' (dēpōnere) its active forms.
Passive endings, active meaning; infinitive -ārī / -ērī / -ī / -īrī; never translate as 'is …-ed'.

*laudātur* and *sequitur* end alike, but *laudātur* is the passive (the 'is done' form) — he is praised — while *sequitur* means *he follows* and can take an object: *Lydia eum sequitur*. A passive-looking verb with an accusative object, or plainly meaning something the subject does, is a deponent. The dictionary form settles it: *laudō* (an active exists) against *sequor*.

more.text: Deponents keep one active-looking form, the present participle: *sequēns* (following), *loquēns* (speaking), *oriēns* (rising). Their commands are the passive shapes — *sequere!* follow!, *sequiminī!* follow, all of you! — a separate skill. Common deponents from chapter XVI: *laetārī* be glad, *verērī* fear, *proficīscī* set out, *opperīrī* wait for, *cōnsōlārī* comfort, *cōnārī* try, *intuērī* look at, *sequī*, *loquī*, *lābī* slip, *complectī* embrace, *ēgredī* go out, *orīrī* rise.

The learner's notes (week 16): deponents are neither active nor passive — their voice is simply deponent; their indicative endings match the passive (*-(i)tur, -(u)ntur*), and the imperative endings *-(e)re* singular, *-(i)minī* plural must be learned now because deponent commands are far commoner than passive ones; the vowel rules are those of regular verbs, but the weak *i*-stems drop the *i*, not the *e*: *ēgredere* (compare *accipe*).

Ørberg (chapter XVI): a deponent is a verb that always has the passive form (except the participle) and stands in the place of an active verb; *laetātur = gaudet, verētur = timet, proficīscitur = abit, opperītur = exspectat*. A&G §190 add the semi-deponents, active in the present but passive in the perfect: *audeō, ausus sum* (dare), *gaudeō, gāvīsus sum*, *soleō, solitus sum* (be used to).
There is no active form to fall back on — the dictionary lists them by the passive-looking first person: *sequor, loquor, cōnor, vereor*.
